title: Agentic Architecture
goal: Given a production scenario, decide the architecture that actually fits: a stop_reason-driven loop, a hub-and-spoke coordinator, a prompt or a programmatic gate, and the right resume, fork or fresh-start call. The loop must branch on stop_reason, preserve history mutations, and handle pause_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded.

steps.title: An agent is a while loop, not a program
steps.inshort: An agentic loop calls the model, runs whatever tools it asked for, appends the results, and calls the model again — repeating until the model stops asking for tools.
steps.lead: Start with the piece that everything else in this domain hangs off. Your code sends a request, Claude replies, and if the reply asks for a tool you run it and send the result back. That cycle is the agent. Everything the exam asks about stopping, gating, delegating or recovering is a decision made somewhere on this cycle.
points: The Messages API is stateless: every call must resend the whole conversation, because the endpoint remembers nothing between requests.
A response is a list of content blocks plus a `stop_reason` field — not a single string of text.
A tool call arrives as a `tool_use` block; you answer it with a `tool_result` block inside a new user-role message.
Each `tool_result` must carry the `tool_use_id` from the matching `tool_use` request, or the model cannot pair them up.
steps.caption: Watch the third card: `stop_reason` is read there, and it is the only thing that decides whether a fourth call happens.
steps.code:
while True:
    response = client.messages.create(model=M, messages=messages, tools=tools)
    messages.append({"role": "assistant", "content": response.content})
    if response.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    results = [run_tool(b) for b in response.content if b.type == "tool_use"]
    messages.append({"role": "user", "content": results})
steps.why: The loop has no built-in sense of completion. The model cannot end your program for you — it can only say what it wants next, and the API gives you one structured field that says whether it wants a tool or is finished. Control lives in your code, driven by that field.
steps.contrast: People reach for natural language: check whether the reply text contains done, or set a fixed iteration cap and call it completion detection. Both look like they work in a demo, because a demo has one happy path. In production the model writes text and calls a tool in the same response, so any check on the text fires early.
steps.exam: This is the foundation task, and most Domain 1 questions reduce to it. If you can state that `stop_reason` is the only authoritative loop-control signal, you can answer the stopping questions without knowing the scenario.
steps.takeaway: The model asks, your code decides. `stop_reason` is the switch.

steps.title: One field decides whether the loop continues
steps.inshort: `stop_reason == "tool_use"` means keep looping. `stop_reason == "end_turn"` means stop. Nothing else decides.
steps.lead: Two values do all the work, and the exam tests the pair constantly. Read the field, not the prose.
points: `tool_use` — the model wants a tool run. Execute it and loop again.
`end_turn` — the model is finished. Exit the loop and return the answer.
`max_tokens` and `stop_sequence` are also stopping states you must handle, because the task may not be done.
`refusal` means the model declined, which is not the same as finishing successfully.
steps.caption: The cycle your code owns. The back edge exists only while stop_reason says tool_use.
steps.why: Because it is a structured field produced by the API rather than text produced by the model, it cannot be reworded, reformatted, or buried in a long explanation. It is the one signal your code can branch on without guessing.
steps.contrast: Parsing the assistant text is the temptation — it avoids one API call and looks cheap. But a single response can carry both a text block and a `tool_use` block, so a text-based check exits while tools are still pending. That is the classic premature-termination bug.
steps.exam: The exam's preferred answer is `stop_reason`-driven control, and it usually appears next to a distractor that sounds more efficient. The other stopping states are tested as a secondary detail.
steps.takeaway: Branch on the field. If it is not `tool_use`, your loop is finished looping.

steps.title: The full stop_reason decision table
steps.inshort: The exam keys tool_use and end_turn, but production loops must also handle pause_turn, max_tokens, stop_sequence, refusal, and model_context_window_exceeded.
steps.lead: Treat any value other than end_turn as not finished, then branch on the specific reason. The two-value loop is the exam foundation; the full table is what keeps production running.
points: tool_use — execute the requested tools, append a single user turn of matching tool_result blocks, and call the API again.
end_turn — the model is finished. Return the final text blocks to the caller.
pause_turn — the server hit its own sampling cap while running server tools. Append the assistant response unchanged and call again with the same tools.
max_tokens — output was truncated. If the last block is tool_use, the JSON input is incomplete: retry with a higher max_tokens.
stop_sequence — output matched your custom stop string. Treat it as a terminal stop for that pattern and finalize per your protocol.
refusal — the model declined for safety reasons. Do not loop; surface the refusal, optionally rephrase, route to a different model, or escalate.
model_context_window_exceeded — the response filled the model's context window. Handle it like max_tokens truncation: continue, summarize, or compact.
steps.caption: Two rows carry the exam; the middle three are what keeps production running when a response stops for any other reason.
steps.why: The exam tests the two-value pair, but the live Messages API returns more states. A loop that only checks tool_use and end_turn silently truncates real work.
steps.contrast: Assuming every non-end_turn response is tool_use is the classic production bug. pause_turn has no tool_result for you to synthesize, and max_tokens with an incomplete tool_use cannot be retried with the same limit.
steps.exam: Given a stop_reason value, identify the correct loop action: continue with tool results, append-and-resend for pause_turn, exit on end_turn, retry-with-larger-budget on max_tokens mid-tool, or surface refusal.
steps.takeaway: end_turn is the only finish signal. Everything else is a specific recovery path.

steps.title: Model-driven decision-making beats a hard-coded tool sequence
steps.inshort: In an agentic loop, Claude reads the current context and decides which tool to call next. A pre-configured decision tree statically runs tool_a → tool_b → tool_c.
steps.lead: This is the difference between an agent and a workflow. The model picks the next step from what it observed; your code only executes the choice.
points: The model, not your code, decides which tool to call next based on the running context.
Agentic loops flex around edge cases the developer never mapped out.
Pre-configured decision trees are fine when the path is known and business logic demands deterministic compliance.
When financial, security, or regulatory rules require a fixed path, programmatic enforcement overrides model flexibility.
steps.caption: Top-right adapts to novel input; bottom-left is a workflow — and a compliance path is pushed back into code by enforcement.
steps.why: The exam favours model-driven approaches because they adapt. Hard-coded sequences are workflows, not agents.
steps.contrast: Calling read_file → search → write_file from your own code with no model-in-the-loop reasoning is a workflow. It is fine for a known path, but it cannot recover from novel inputs.
steps.exam: Distinguish model-driven decision-making from pre-configured decision trees, and pick the right pattern for the described task: open-ended task = agent; well-defined fixed path = workflow.
steps.takeaway: Let the model decide when the path is open. Enforce in code when the path is a compliance requirement.

steps.title: The history mutation rule: append, then append again
steps.inshort: Between iterations, append the assistant turn verbatim (including tool_use blocks), then append one user turn whose content is only tool_result blocks keyed by tool_use_id.
steps.lead: This is the critical handoff in the loop. Miss either mutation and the next request is invalid or the model cannot see what the tool returned.
points: Append the assistant turn verbatim — the tool_use blocks must survive into history.
Then append a single new user turn whose content is a list of tool_result blocks, one per tool_use_id.
Do not add extra text after tool_result blocks; trailing text teaches Claude to expect user text after every tool call and causes empty end_turn responses.
The Messages API is stateless: every request must carry the full history, because the endpoint remembers nothing between calls.
steps.caption: Watch the two appends: assistant verbatim, then a pure tool_result user turn. Miss either one and the next request is invalid.
steps.why: Sending tool results without first appending the assistant tool_use turn produces an invalid messages array and an API error. The pairing is the contract.
steps.contrast: The common bug is to send only the tool_result, or to synthesize a result for pause_turn. pause_turn has no result to synthesize — resend the assistant content unchanged.
steps.exam: Identify which messages mutations are required between iterations: append assistant turn verbatim, then append a user turn of tool_result blocks keyed by tool_use_id.
steps.takeaway: Verbatim assistant first. Pure tool_result user turn second.

steps.title: Anti-pattern one: parsing natural language for completion
steps.inshort: Checking if the reply contains words like "done" or "finished" to decide whether to stop the loop.
steps.lead: It feels intuitive and works in early testing. It is also the most brittle choice you can make.
points: Natural language is ambiguous — the model might narrate reasoning ("let me check that") without calling a tool, or call a tool with no narration.
Phrasing drifts across prompts and model versions — a string match that works today silently breaks tomorrow.
The structured contract does not drift: a turn that wants a tool returns `stop_reason: tool_use`, full stop.
steps.caption: The left check fails both ways — too early when the model narrates, never when its wording changes.

ask.q: A support agent loops over `client.messages.create` with tools. A teammate proposes exiting the loop whenever the assistant text contains the words done or resolved, to save an API call. Production shows the agent sometimes stops mid-task with a partial answer. What is the bug?
options: A) The model sometimes narrates reasoning without emitting a tool call, so the text check fires early
B) The model stops emitting the word done after a prompt tweak, so the loop runs forever
C) Both A and B
D) The API ignores the text and only respects stop_reason

steps.why: Prose parsing fails both ways: it stops early when the model narrates, and runs forever when the model's wording changes.
steps.contrast: A string match looks deterministic in a test case. In production the model's wording is not a contract.
steps.exam: The exam will phrase this as a production symptom — partial answers, infinite loops — and ask which change you would ship. The fix is always: branch on stop_reason.
steps.takeaway: Text is for humans. stop_reason is for code.

steps.title: Anti-pattern two: iteration caps as the primary stopping mechanism
steps.inshort: Running a fixed number of iterations and returning whatever you have, instead of checking stop_reason.
steps.lead: Capping iterations is a legitimate safety guard. The anti-pattern is using that cap as the primary way to decide the work is done.
points: If your loop's real stopping logic is "run exactly five iterations," you cut off useful work when the task needed six, and waste turns when it finished in two.
The cap is blind to whether the model is actually finished.
The correct design branches on `stop_reason` to decide completion, and keeps a generous iteration cap only as a backstop against runaways.
Caps guard; they do not decide.
steps.caption: Look at where the stop happens: at the cap, not at end_turn — and the task that needed one more turn is truncated.
steps.code:
# guard, not decision
MAX_ITER = 50  # generous backstop
while iter < MAX_ITER:
    resp = client.messages.create(...)
    if resp.stop_reason != "tool_use":
        break
    # ... run tools, append results
    iter += 1
# iter == MAX_ITER means something went wrong — alert, don't silently return
steps.why: A cap that is also the completion logic produces two failure modes: truncation (task needed more turns) and waste (task finished early). Both are invisible until you check results.
steps.contrast: Setting MAX_ITER=5 looks safe in a demo where tasks finish in 3. In production the distribution shifts.
steps.exam: Expect a scenario where an agent "sometimes returns incomplete answers." The trap answer is "increase the cap." The fix is: branch on stop_reason, keep a generous cap as a guardrail.
steps.takeaway: Caps are guardrails. stop_reason is the decision.

steps.title: Anti-pattern three: checking for assistant text as a completion signal
steps.inshort: If the assistant returned a text block, conclude the agent is finished.
steps.lead: This breaks because the model frequently emits a text block alongside a `tool_use` block, narrating what it is about to do while also requesting the tool.
points: Seeing text present, your loop concludes the agent is done, returns the half-formed narration, and never runs the tool.
This is the bug at the heart of premature loop termination: checking `response.content[0].type == "text"` ends the loop early.
The presence of text tells you nothing definitive about completion. Only `stop_reason` does.
steps.caption: One response can carry narration and a tool_use block together — the shape check returns the narration and never runs the tool.
steps.why: A single response can contain both text narration and tool_use blocks. The text narrates intent; stop_reason declares completion.
steps.contrast: The content array describes what the model produced. stop_reason describes what the model intends next.
steps.exam: The exam shows a loop that checks for text blocks and asks why it fails on multi-step tasks. The answer: text and tool_use can appear together.

steps.title: Three wrong signals versus the one right signal
steps.inshort: Every anti-pattern routes the decision through a proxy; only stop_reason is authoritative.
steps.lead: The sound loop is a while driven by stop_reason: continue while tool_use, stop on end_turn, explicitly handle max_tokens and refusal. A safety cap is a guardrail, never the primary logic.
points: Natural-language parsing trusts wording
Iteration caps trust a counter
Content-type checks trust block shape
None of those proxies is the model's actual statement of intent
steps.caption: Only the bottom row is the model's own statement of intent — the three rows above it are guesses your loop cannot verify.
steps.why: The unifying fix for all three anti-patterns is single: read stop_reason and branch on it.
steps.contrast: New variations appear constantly ("stop when response < 50 tokens", "stop after particular tool"). All fail the same way: they trust a proxy. If you can ask "Is this decision made by stop_reason or a proxy for it?" you can classify any loop on sight.
steps.exam: When the exam shows four loop designs, the right one branches on stop_reason and treats caps as backstops. The three wrong ones each lean on an anti-pattern.
steps.takeaway: Structured signal over prose, one authoritative field over three proxies.

steps.title: When one agent stops being enough
steps.inshort: A single agent fails in two named ways: its context window fills before the work finishes, and it produces generic output because one agent cannot specialise.
steps.lead: A research analyst runs one Claude agent that plans the search, reads the sources, synthesises and writes the deck. On a two-source brief it is excellent. On a forty-source engagement it starts strong, then repeats searches it already ran, forgets findings it made an hour ago, and delivers a summary that could have been written without reading anything. Nothing crashed. It hit two ceilings at once.
points: The context ceiling: the window fills before the task completes, so earlier findings fall out and the agent loses the thread of its own work.
The specialization gap: one agent carrying every role produces generic work, because it cannot be tuned for discovery and for synthesis at the same time.
The exam's first move is always to test whether either trigger is really present — if neither is, a single agent is the correct answer.
Splitting is not free: each subagent is another context to fill, another failure to handle, another result to reconcile.
steps.caption: Both halves of the failure are present at once — relieving only one ceiling leaves the agent still broken.
steps.why: Those two triggers are the justification the exam expects. "The task felt big" is not a trigger; a measured context ceiling or a demonstrable specialization gap is.
steps.contrast: Teams split into multi-agent because the task sounds impressive, then spend the budget on orchestration instead of work. The distractors here are usually proportionate-looking fixes to a system that should never have been split, or a split that was never given a coordinator.
steps.exam: Scenario items hand you a failing single agent and ask what to change first. The answer names the trigger — relieve the context, or split the role — never "add more agents" as a reflex.
steps.takeaway: Split for a named reason: a context ceiling or a specialization gap.

steps.title: Which fix actually addresses the failure?
steps.lead: You are reviewing the failing engagement above and must choose the remediation.
steps.caption: The left column asks the agent to recover or outlast lost context; only the right column keeps each context small.

ask.q: A single Claude agent handles a competitive-research engagement: it plans the search, reads sources, synthesises and writes the deck. Late in the engagement it starts repeating searches it already ran, and its final synthesis misses two topics it had covered early on. Which approach is most effective?
options: Increase the agent's iteration cap so it keeps working until every topic is covered.
Raise the model tier for the whole run so the agent reasons better across the long engagement.
Split the work so a coordinator holds the topic plan and spawns scoped subagents that return structured findings.
Add a prompt instruction telling the agent to re-read its earlier findings before synthesising.
ask.why: The signature is a context ceiling: work done early has fallen out of the window, so it is repeated and then missed. A coordinator holding the plan centrally, with scoped subagents keeping each context small, fixes the cause. A (a larger iteration cap) lets it work longer inside a broken context. B (a higher model tier) does not change window pressure and spends cost. D asks the agent to recover material that is no longer in its context — it cannot.

steps.title: Hub-and-spoke: one control point
steps.inshort: One coordinator decomposes, selects, passes context, aggregates, validates and recovers. Subagents never talk to each other.
steps.lead: The coordinator is the only component that sees the whole job. It decides whether to spawn at all, how many subagents, which ones, and what each is told. Results come back to it, and it is the component that reconciles contradictions before anything reaches the user.
points: Every hop routes through the coordinator — a subagent handing results straight to another subagent removes the one place where errors are handled uniformly.
Decomposition quality is the coordinator's job: a narrow plan produces missing topics no matter how good the subagents are.
Aggregation means synthesis, not concatenation — raw subagent outputs pasted together carry contradictions and overlap into the deliverable.
Hierarchy is permitted: a subagent may spawn its own subagents when its definition allows it, and the control-point rule still holds at every level.
steps.caption: Watch the absence of arrows between the spokes — subagents never talk to each other; every hop routes through the hub.
steps.why: A single control point is what makes partial failure visible and error handling uniform. Remove it and failures stay invisible until the output is already wrong.
steps.contrast: The tempting design is peer-to-peer subagents "collaborating" through shared live state to avoid duplicate work. Subagents run in isolated contexts and cannot watch each other mid-flight, so the mechanism cannot do what it promises.
steps.exam: Multi-agent items are usually scope failures at the coordinator, not execution failures at the subagents. The question tests whether you blame the right component.
steps.takeaway: One coordinator, many isolated subagents, everything routed through the hub.

steps.title: The subagent that returns something generic
steps.lead: A coordinator has just spawned a subagent and received a disappointing result.
steps.caption: The subagent sees only these children — any fact the coordinator leaves out of the spawn is invisible to it.

ask.q: A coordinator spawns a market-analysis subagent with the instruction "analyse the market for our new product". The subagent returns a generic essay that ignores the client's segment, the two competitors already identified, and the pricing constraint. Which approach is most effective?
options: Rewrite the subagent's instruction to demand specific, data-backed analysis in a stricter tone.
Give the subagent web search and a document reader so it can find the missing detail itself.
Put the segment, the two named competitors and the pricing constraint into the subagent's agent definition at spawn time.
Add a coordinator step that reviews each subagent output and re-prompts it until it becomes specific.
ask.why: Context does not inherit: a subagent knows only what its definition carries, so missing detail is an injection failure at the coordinator and the fix belongs there. A (stricter wording) asks the subagent to produce facts it was never given. B (more tools) adds capability without adding context. D (review and re-prompt) pays a round trip to recover information that should have been in the spawn.

steps.title: Spawning: the Task tool and the agent definition
steps.inshort: The coordinator spawns subagents by calling the Task tool with a strict agent definition — description, prompt, tools, optionally model. Without Task in allowedTools, delegation is physically impossible.
steps.lead: In Claude Code and the Agent SDK the mechanism is a tool call: the coordinator emits a Task (Agent) call carrying a definition object. Everything about the subagent is decided at that moment — what it is for, what it is told, what it may touch, and which model runs it.
points: The definition's description is the selection signal — write it like a function docstring, because the coordinator chooses subagents by it.
The prompt is the subagent's entire universe: it inherits no conversation, so every fact it needs must be written into the definition.
Tools are scoped per subagent: a synthesis agent that only checks facts gets a narrow verify tool, not web search.
Task must appear in the coordinator's allowedTools; subagents need it only when they spawn their own.
Parallel spawning means several spawn calls in ONE coordinator response — separate turns run them sequentially.
steps.caption: Read top down: without the first band nothing spawns, and the middle bands are the entire world the subagent will know.
steps.why: Delegation is a tool call, so it obeys tool-call rules: an unavailable tool cannot be called, and a subagent's behaviour is bounded by the definition it was spawned with.
steps.contrast: The tempting fix for "the orchestrator never delegates" is a prompt instruction to delegate more. If Task is absent from allowedTools, no wording can help — the capability is missing, not the intention.
steps.exam: "The orchestrator never delegates" and "the subagent returned something generic" are single-cause items: a missing allowedTools entry, and missing injected context.
steps.takeaway: Delegation is a tool call with a definition object: allowedTools decides whether it can happen, the definition decides what happens.

steps.title: Diagnose the orchestrator that never delegates
steps.lead: A coordinator in production is not doing the job its prompt describes.
steps.caption: The only branch that reaches delegation is the pass exit — prompt wording, prompt length and iteration caps never cross this gate.

ask.q: A production coordinator is supposed to fan work out to three specialised subagents. Logs show it answers every request itself and has never issued a single spawn call, although its system prompt describes the delegation pattern in detail. Which approach is most effective?
options: Strengthen the prompt with an explicit rule to delegate any request covering more than one research topic.
Add "Task" to the coordinator's allowedTools.
Shorten the coordinator's system prompt so the delegation instructions stand out more.
Raise the coordinator's iteration cap so it has more turns in which to delegate.
ask.why: The Task tool must be in the coordinator's allowedTools or it cannot emit a spawn call at all — the capability is missing, which is exactly why no amount of prompt wording has ever worked. A and C tune instructions that were already sufficient. D adds turns in which the same absent capability stays absent.

steps.title: The subagent's world is the prompt — so make the prompt structured
steps.inshort: A subagent inherits nothing; whatever it needs must be handed over explicitly. Pass findings as a structured object of claims each paired with its source, not as a prose summary.
steps.lead: A coordinator has been running for ten minutes and now spawns a synthesis subagent with “here are the findings from the previous agents, please synthesize them into a report.” The subagent replies, in effect, “what findings?” It has no memory of anything that happened before. It either hallucinates or produces a generic report. This is the number-one mistake in multi-agent architecture, and it looks perfectly reasonable until you watch it fail.
points: Every subagent starts with a clean slate: its entire world is what the coordinator writes into the spawn prompt — no conversation history carries over.
Hand over findings as a structured object: a claims array where each claim carries a claim id, the claim text, a source id and a confidence, plus a sources array keyed by source id.

Pass the whole object — never extract just the claims and drop the sources; the next agent needs both to produce accurate, traceable output. The synthesis prompt should require every claim to cite its source URL and preserve the retrieved-at date.

Conflicts are annotated, never silently resolved: when two sources disagree, add a conflict object carrying both claims with their source ids, mark it unresolved, and escalate to the coordinator, which makes the final call.

Every subagent is itself a full agentic loop — the same stop_reason loop from 1.1, just spawned by the coordinator. In Claude Code and the Agent SDK the spawn is a Task tool call; the raw Anthropic SDK has no Task tool, so the same pattern is reproduced with an ordinary function plus tool schemas.
steps.why: A subagent has no channel to ask a previous subagent or the coordinator's history for missing detail. Structured, self-contained context is the only way the handoff can be accurate — and a claim that loses its source cannot be verified, so a hallucination becomes indistinguishable from a finding.
steps.contrast: The tempting handoff is one line of prose — “here are the research notes, synthesize them” — because it feels sufficient and costs nothing. It costs everything: the subagent does not know what those notes are, so it invents or generalizes, and the source attribution is already gone.
steps.exam: Scenario 3 (Multi-Agent Research System) tests this directly: attribution is lost because web results were summarized into prose before synthesis. The fix is a structured object with explicit claim-to-source mappings; the trap is asking a subagent to re-search or to resolve a conflict itself.
steps.takeaway: The subagent knows only what you hand it. Hand it structured claims with sources, not prose.

steps.title: Where did that claim come from?
steps.lead: A multi-agent research pipeline is producing a report whose claims cannot be traced.

ask.q: A research coordinator has each subagent summarize its web searches into a paragraph, then passes those paragraphs to a synthesis subagent. The final report reads well, but reviewers cannot trace any claim back to a source, and two searches that disagreed were silently merged into one statement. Which approach is most effective?
options: Instruct each subagent to append a list of source URLs at the end of its summary paragraph.
Have the synthesis subagent re-run the web searches so it can re-verify every claim before writing.
Pass findings as a structured object of claims each carrying its source id and confidence, and let the coordinator annotate conflicts and make the final call.
Add a review subagent that checks the final report for unsupported claims and rewrites them.
ask.why: A prose summary destroys provenance before synthesis, and a subagent must never silently resolve a conflict. Structured claim-to-source mappings preserve attribution, and conflicting claims are annotated and escalated to the coordinator for the final decision. A re-attaches sources only at the paragraph level, so no individual claim is traceable. B repeats work and still cannot reconstruct the original sourcing. D cleans the output after the fact, but the provenance is already gone and the merged conflict is already baked in.

steps.title: Prompts are requests; hooks are guarantees
steps.inshort: A system-prompt rule is a request with a non-zero failure rate. When a single failure means financial loss, a security breach or a compliance violation, enforce the rule in code — a hook — not in a prompt.
steps.lead: A customer-support agent's system prompt says “only process refunds under $500.” One day a $2,000 refund comes in, the model weighs the instruction against its own judgment, and processes it anyway. The prompt said no; the model said yes. That gap is the entire reason this task exists.
points: Language models are probabilistic: they follow an instruction most of the time, and most of the time is not a guarantee.
A hook is code that intercepts the agentic loop at a fixed moment and cannot be overridden by the model.
A prompt rule is also easy to under-specify — “don't refund over $500” silently leaves the model free to decide verified customers are exempt.
Exam trigger words — guarantee, must never, policy requires — point at programmatic enforcement, which in Claude Code means a hook.
Deterministic beats probabilistic whenever one failure is unacceptable; tone, style and formatting can safely stay in prompts.
steps.why: For money, identity, safety or compliance, a 99% success rate is a loss, not a success. The model cannot be relied on to obey a rule every time, so the guarantee has to live in code where the model has no vote.
steps.contrast: The tempting fix is a stronger prompt — “you must NEVER process refunds above $500, this is critical” — or few-shot examples of correct behaviour. Both raise the odds; neither gives a guarantee, which is exactly what a high-stakes rule needs.
steps.exam: The highest-frequency fork in the whole exam: a high-stakes rule with four options, three of which are prompt-strengthening moves (stronger wording, few-shot examples, a specialised subagent) and one of which is a hook. The hook is always the answer.
steps.takeaway: Prompts persuade. Hooks guarantee. Put money, identity, safety and compliance in code.

steps.title: The refund that ran before verification
steps.lead: A support agent is supposed to verify a customer before refunding, and occasionally does not.

ask.q: A support agent's system prompt tells it to always call get_customer to verify identity before calling process_refund, and shows three worked examples of the correct order. Production logs show process_refund occasionally running first for unverified customers. Which change most reliably fixes this?
options: Add a stronger, capitalised instruction at the top of the system prompt forbidding refunds for unverified customers.
Add more few-shot examples covering edge cases of the verification-first order.
Add a PreToolUse prerequisite gate that blocks process_refund until get_customer has run and set a verified flag.
Give the coordinator a separate verification subagent and instruct it to run first.
ask.why: Ordering that must always hold is a deterministic requirement, so it belongs in code. A PreToolUse prerequisite gate physically blocks the downstream tool until the upstream tool has succeeded and set a verified flag — the model cannot skip it. A and B add more probabilistic instruction to a rule that already had both wording and examples. D moves the check into a subagent's prompt, which is still a request the model can ignore.

steps.title: Two interception points — and the verified flag
steps.inshort: PreToolUse fires before a tool runs and can block or skip it — use it for policy and prerequisites. PostToolUse fires after the tool but before the model sees the result — use it to normalize, redact or enrich the raw output.
steps.lead: Picture the loop: the model asks for a tool, the tool runs, the result goes back. Hooks let you drop code into the two seams of that cycle. One seam catches the call on the way in; the other catches the result on the way out.
points: PreToolUse intercepts before execution: check prerequisites, enforce a policy, or block the call outright — e.g. refuse a refund over $500 and escalate to a human instead of ever running process_refund.
PostToolUse runs on the raw result before the model reads it: map database codes (status 3/5/8) to English, convert an epoch value to a date, redact or truncate.
A hook must be a pass-through for every tool it does not care about — early-return the raw result unchanged when the tool name does not match.
Prerequisite gates are PreToolUse hooks that track session state: block a downstream tool (lookup_order, process_refund) until an upstream tool (get_customer) has succeeded and set a verified flag.

That flag is set by a companion PostToolUse hook — once get_customer finds the customer, the hook flips session.customer_verified to true, and the gate reads it before allowing anything downstream. The same precondition can be enforced one level up: the coordinator does not spawn the refund subagent if verification reported no such customer.
steps.why: The two seams are where determinism lives. Gating before execution prevents the wrong action; normalizing after execution means the model reasons over clean, consistent data instead of raw database values. The verified flag is what turns “please verify first” into a rule the model cannot break.
steps.contrast: Teams normalize downstream in reporting code, or capture prior state in a PostToolUse hook after the mutation already happened. Both miss the seam: the model needs clean input before it reasons, and prior state has to be read before the tool changes it.
steps.exam: Two keyword triggers decide these items — policy / must not run / prerequisite / “before X happens” → PreToolUse; heterogeneous formats / normalize / “the model is confused by varying outputs” → PostToolUse. The canonical stem is “the agent occasionally calls process_refund before get_customer.”
steps.takeaway: Gate before the tool runs; normalize after it runs; let a verified flag decide whether a downstream tool may run at all.

steps.title: The tool that returns database codes
steps.lead: A lookup tool hands the model raw rows.

ask.q: A customer-support agent's lookup_order tool returns raw database rows: numeric status codes (3, 5, 8) and an epoch timestamp. The model keeps misreading order status and occasionally reports a delivered order as pending. Which change is most effective?
options: Add a PostToolUse hook on lookup_order that maps the status codes to readable labels and the epoch value to a date before the model sees the result.
Add a PreToolUse hook that blocks lookup_order until the database returns normalized values.
Rewrite the system prompt to explain what each numeric status code means.
Add a reporting step that translates the statuses after the agent has finished reasoning.
ask.why: This is a normalization problem at the tool boundary, which is exactly what PostToolUse is for — the hook transforms the raw result before the model reads it. B gates execution, but the tool is not the problem; its output format is, so blocking it changes nothing. C asks the model to translate codes it will still sometimes misread. D normalizes after the model has already reasoned over bad data, so the misreading has already happened.

steps.title: Do you know the steps before you start?
steps.inshort: If you know the exact steps up front, chain them in a fixed sequence. If the next step depends on what the last one revealed, let the agent generate the steps dynamically.
steps.lead: Before you design an agentic workflow, the exam asks the same question you should ask yourself: do I know the steps before I start? The answer picks the pattern, not a preference.
points: Prompt chaining breaks the task into a predefined sequence — output of step one feeds step two, like an assembly line. Ideal for compliance, reproducibility and known pipelines (a CI/CD or PR-review flow).

Dynamic decomposition generates the next step from what was found. You supply a goal and generic tools (read logs, query DB, check config, trace request), not a fixed script — the right fit for a production incident whose cause is unknown until you look.
The warning is the exam's trap: never use prompt chaining for an open-ended task, because the predefined steps become wrong the moment findings diverge from the initial assumptions.

Chaining lives inside subagents too — a coordinator that always spawns verify → process in order is itself a chained workflow, and a subagent's own loop can be chained internally when its steps are known. The choice is per-workflow, not global.
The decision rule is one line: known path → chain; evidence-driven path → adapt.
steps.why: A fixed pipeline applied to an unknown cause walks steps that do not fit, spends the budget, and still misses the real root cause; a dynamic loop applied to a fixed compliance path is unpredictable. Match the shape of the work.
steps.contrast: The tempting move is to run a fixed checklist unconditionally “just in case,” or to brute-force every layer in parallel. Both spend budget without following the evidence.
steps.exam: The discriminating scenario is always the shape of the work — “every request follows the same flow” is chaining; “the cause is unknown until we investigate” is dynamic decomposition.
steps.takeaway: Known steps → chain them. Unknown steps → let the findings decide the next step.

steps.title: The intermittent production bug
steps.lead: An agent is asked to investigate a bug nobody can reproduce.

ask.q: An agent must find the root cause of an intermittent production bug. The cause is unknown, and the next step depends on what the investigation reveals. Which decomposition strategy fits?
options: Prompt chaining with a fixed checklist: read logs, then query the database, then check config, then write a report.
Dynamic decomposition: start from the last 24 hours of error logs and let each finding decide the next investigation step.
A fixed pipeline that runs every diagnostic step in parallel regardless of what earlier steps find.
A single-pass prompt that asks the model to output the root cause immediately.
ask.why: An unknown cause is the textbook dynamic-decomposition case: the next step depends on what the last one revealed. A is a fixed checklist run on an unknown path — the steps may not fit and the real cause can be missed. C spends budget on layers the evidence does not point to. D skips investigation entirely and invites a hallucinated root cause.

steps.title: Resume, fork, or start clean
steps.inshort: Resume a named session only while its context is still valid; fork a shared baseline to explore parallel approaches without touching the original; start fresh when the tool results are stale and inject a prior-findings summary as a hypothesis to validate.
steps.lead: You have a session that did good work, and the instinct is to keep it because it was expensive. Before you reuse it, ask two things: what changed since, and what am I about to do with it?
points: Named resume: start a session with a name and later continue it by that name (--resume <name>; bare --resume picks the most recent). Always state explicitly what changed since — the agent cannot detect modified files, updated dependencies or new requirements on its own.

Fork: resume a session under a new id so the original is untouched, giving two branches the same expensive baseline while each explores a different approach. Fork is for parallel exploration only — not for absorbing targeted file edits.
Fresh start has two triggers: the prior tool results are fundamentally stale (a heavily changed codebase), or extended context degrades the model's reasoning capability.
When starting fresh, give the new session a structured summary of prior findings — and frame it as a hypothesis to validate, not as established fact.
Never resume a session with a heavily changed codebase, and never resume without telling the agent what changed.
steps.why: Resuming is cheaper, which is exactly why it is dangerous: acting on stale tool results produces confidently wrong work that costs more than a fresh start. The validity of the prior context — not the sunk cost — decides.
steps.contrast: The instinct is to resume because the work was expensive. But if most of the codebase changed, the context is no longer valid, and the cheap option is the wrong one. A fork does not help either, because both branches inherit the same stale baseline.
steps.exam: Scenario 2 (Code Generation) tests the fork in the road: analysis ran a few days ago and one module was refactored → resume with explicit change info; it ran long ago with several modules changed → fresh session plus a hypothesis-framed summary.
steps.takeaway: Resume while context is valid, fork to branch from a shared baseline, start fresh when the results are stale — and always say what changed.

steps.title: The session from eight months ago
steps.lead: A long analysis session is being considered for reuse.

ask.q: A codebase-analysis session ran eight months ago and its findings are stored. Since then the team rewrote most of the service and migrated to a new framework. The agent now needs to add a feature in that service. What is the best approach?
options: Resume the session with --resume so the agent keeps all of its earlier analysis and adds the new feature.
Fork the session so the new work shares the old session's baseline context.
Start a fresh session and inject a structured summary of the prior findings framed as hypotheses to validate against the current code.
Resume the session and trust the agent to notice the changed files as it reads them.
ask.why: The prior tool results are stale — most of the service changed — so resuming means the agent reasons over outdated analysis. A fresh session with a structured, hypothesis-framed summary keeps the valid findings without importing the stale ones. A resumes on stale context. B forks, but a fork inherits the same stale baseline, and fork is for exploring parallel approaches, not for absorbing a rewrite. D assumes the agent detects changes it cannot.

steps.title: Check your understanding
steps.inshort: An agent occasionally returns an empty or half-written answer. Its loop ends as soon as the assistant response includes any text content block.
steps.lead: Identify the anti-pattern and the fix.
steps.caption: Follow the narrowing: only the bottom band touches the root cause — the other three options leave the completion logic untouched.

ask.q: An agent occasionally returns an empty or half-written answer. Its loop ends as soon as the assistant response includes any text content block. What is the best fix?
options: A) Stop using text-block presence as the completion signal and branch the loop on `stop_reason` instead
B) Add a longer system-prompt instruction telling Claude to always finish before replying
C) Lower `max_tokens` so the model produces shorter, more decisive responses
D) Retry the request automatically whenever the answer looks short

steps.why: The bug is anti-pattern three: checking for text presence instead of stop_reason. The model emits text alongside tool_use. Only A addresses the root cause.
steps.contrast: B relies on prompting (probabilistic). C truncates answers (counterproductive). D papers over the bug without fixing the logic.
steps.exam: This exact question structure appears: a production symptom, four fixes, one structural and three superficial.
steps.takeaway: The fix is always: read stop_reason.

steps.title: Exam lens — the one question that decides every Domain 1 loop answer
steps.inshort: Ask: "Does this make the loop more dependent on stop_reason or less?"
steps.lead: Answers that add prose parsing, lean harder on a counter, or inspect content shape all move away from the authoritative signal and are wrong by construction. The single answer that moves toward branching on stop_reason, even if phrased plainly, is the one to choose.
points: Prose parsing → less dependent on stop_reason → wrong
Iteration cap as primary logic → less dependent on stop_reason → wrong
Content-type check → less dependent on stop_reason → wrong
Branch on stop_reason, cap as guardrail → more dependent on stop_reason → correct
steps.caption: Send every option through this gate: pass if it branches on stop_reason, fail if it trusts a proxy for the field.
steps.why: This lens collapses a four-option question into a one-question test. It is the same lens you should apply when reviewing real agent code.
steps.contrast: Most wrong answers in Domain 1 add a moving part: another agent, another cap, another prompt clause. The pattern is to prefer the signal that already exists and the guarantee that cannot be argued with.
steps.exam: Expect the scenario to describe a production symptom and ask which change you would ship. Sort the options by whether they add a probability or a guarantee.
steps.takeaway: Stop_reason is the source of truth. Every other signal is a proxy.
